analysis.one_liner: Bars federal agencies from finalizing rules that could cut oil, gas, or biofuel production or raise gasoline prices.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with 7 Republican cosponsors, was referred to two House committees and a subcommittee, and died without ever receiving a committee or floor vote before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped federal agencies from finalizing any rule that would reduce domestic oil, gas, or biofuel production, raise gasoline prices, or have any negative effect on energy production, electricity generation, fuel or power transmission, infrastructure, or transportation fuels [S2, S3]. The freeze would have lasted until either January 1, 2023, or the day the national average gasoline price hit $2.60 per gallon, whichever came first [S2, S3]. It was pitched as pump-price relief but its main effect would have been a temporary moratorium on new energy and environmental regulations, which primarily protects producers [S2, S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Oil, gas, coal, and biofuel producers benefit most: for months, no new federal rule could be finalized if it would cut their production, raise their costs, or otherwise disadvantage them. Drivers would benefit only if halting new rules actually lowered pump prices, which the bill asserts but which depends heavily on global oil markets beyond any agency's control.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil, gas, coal, and biofuel producers

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any federal agency from finalizing a rule that would decrease domestic oil, gas, or biofuel production or increase gasoline prices.
Broadens that ban to any rule causing negative effects on domestic energy production, electricity generation, transmission, infrastructure, or transportation fuels.
Sets the freeze to end when the national average gasoline price reaches $2.60 per gallon or on January 1, 2023, whichever comes first.

analysis.who_pays: The public pays through a freeze on new energy and environmental rules, meaning delayed limits on pollution and updated protections would not take effect during the freeze period. Consumers bear that cost while the promised relief at the pump is uncertain, because gasoline prices are driven substantially by global crude oil supply, not just domestic regulation.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, via delayed environmental and consumer rules

drawbacks.text: The ban sweeps extremely broadly: it covers not just rules that raise prices but any rule with any negative effect on energy production, generation, or infrastructure, which could block pollution limits, safety updates, and climate-related rules alike.

The $2.60 per gallon trigger sat far below the prices drivers were actually paying when the bill was introduced, meaning the regulatory freeze could have lasted the entire window and accomplished little for pump prices.

Because gasoline prices move mainly with global crude markets, halting new domestic rules does not guarantee lower prices for drivers, so the public cost (a rules freeze) could come without the promised benefit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to drivers is speculative and likely small, since prices at the pump track world oil markets as much as domestic rules. The cost is concrete: a months-long ban on finalizing energy and environmental rules, written broadly enough to cover nearly any new restriction on producers. On balance, the bill's design serves producers more reliably than it serves consumers.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in two House committees after referral, was sent to a subcommittee in November 2022, and never got a markup or floor vote before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Representative Michelle Fischbach introduced the bill on March 31, 2022, with seven Republican cosponsors.
The same day, it was referred to the House Oversight and Reform Committee and the House Judiciary Committee.
On November 1, 2022, the Judiciary Committee referred it to its Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law Subcommittee.
No further action was taken; neither committee advanced the bill, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, no regulatory freeze took effect, so agencies kept their authority to finalize energy and environmental rules and the public kept existing avenues for new protections. Oil and gas producers avoided a floor vote on a measure that would have shielded them, but they also gained nothing from it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Agencies and the public, as no freeze took effect

for.name: Rep. Michelle Fischbach
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Gas Prices Relief Act of 2022 on March 31, 2022.

for.name: 7 House Republican cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (Reps. Newhouse, Miller-Meeks, Pfluger, Davis, Estes, LaMalfa, and Stauber).

against.name: House Oversight and Reform and Judiciary Committee chairs
against.role: Chairs of the two committees of referral (majority Democrats in the 117th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup or a floor vote; it received only a subcommittee referral and no further action.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all seven cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat supported it, and the Democratic majority committees never advanced it.

industries.note: The bill would have barred any new rule that cuts their production, raises their costs, or otherwise disadvantages them for the freeze period. Drivers get only an uncertain price benefit that depends mostly on global oil markets, while pollution and safety rules would be frozen alongside it.
Named directly in the bill's ban on rules that would decrease production, giving biofuels the same shield from new restrictions as oil and gas.
The ban covers any rule with negative effects on domestic electricity generation and transmission, which would shield fossil power plants from new federal requirements during the freeze.
